When @Starlink helped save a man’s life during emergency surgery in rural Zimbabwe.

A young man suffered severe burns to his leg after falling into a cooking fire during a seizure. His parents spent hours helping him reach a remote hospital in Chisizya.

Dr. Mike Jeans needed to perform an emergency operation he had never done before. Using Starlink, he called a colleague in South Africa, who guided him through the surgery.

The operation succeeded. The patient was transferred by ambulance to a larger hospital. MATTER, the charity involved, reported that he survived and was recovering.

Starlink connected a doctor to lifesaving medical guidance when his patient needed it most.

This is why Starlink matters. A working connection can help save a life. This lifesaving technology should be available in every part of the world.

In the summer of 1994, a 23-year-old Elon Musk spent his days in Los Gatos at Pinnacle Research Institute, dreaming up how ultracapacitors could power electric cars and even Star Wars–style laser guns. Then, around 5 p.m. every evening, he drove to Palo Alto for his second job at Rocket Science Games, a startup full of future legends, from Tony Fadell, who would later build the iPod, to the people behind Apple's QuickTime and engineers from Industrial Light & Magic. 

They hired him to write the most boring code imaginable, drivers so joysticks and mice would work with games, but Elon quietly gave himself a much harder problem 😂: figuring out how a computer could run a game and stream video from a CD at the same time, something the machines of that era simply couldn't do. 

Peter Barrett, one of the company's founders, remembered him as "completely unflappable," and said that after a while nobody was giving him directions at all, because he was just building what he wanted to build. Bruce Leak, who hired him, said: "He had boundless energy." So yeah, nobody handed Elon the big problem, he just went looking for it, at night, after a full day at another job. This is who Elon Musk is 💙

Zuckerberg admitted the fact checkers he paid for 8 years destroyed more trust than they created, replacing them with Community Notes after calling them too politically biased. 

Facebook launched the program right after Trump’s 2016 win, paying outlets like PolitiFact to rate posts and slap reduced reach plus warning screens on anything they marked false. 

Musk took the opposite path when he turned Birdwatch into Community Notes, where notes only surface after people who normally disagree both rate them helpful. 

TikTok and YouTube later rolled out their own crowd written versions. 

Professional fact checking was pitched as the fix for misinformation, but once its biggest client walked away, the industry’s rivals started copying the model instead.

quote.author: Rothmus
quote.name: Rothmus 🏴
quote.text:
Elon fired roughly 80% of Twitter’s staff without crashing the site the way every “expert” swore it would. 

After the November 2022 cuts and the “hardcore” ultimatum that drove hundreds of engineers out the door, the remaining team handled record World Cup traffic that was supposed to break the platform. 

When Musk later told the BBC the cuts were painful but necessary to avoid bankruptcy, the results were already clear. 
Zuckerberg watched it happen, called 2023 Meta’s “year of efficiency,” and cut about 21,000 jobs while saying the leaner Twitter was probably good for the industry. 

4 years later, X still runs on a fraction of the old headcount, which shows the large staff everyone religiously believed was essential was mostly optional the entire time.
